units.text: Start with the Regions column on the left. A Region offers a broad set of managed services and resilience options. Evaluate data location and application requirements before selecting the compute platform.

Move to Local Zones. Supported resources sit closer to users, while remaining connected to a parent Region. Check the location's available services and the complete application path before expecting lower latency.

Now examine Outposts. AWS-managed infrastructure sits in your facility. The design still depends on suitable power, space, networking and regional connectivity; local placement does not remove those responsibilities.

With the full slide visible, compare customer-managed on-premises compute on the right. It gives local control with more operational responsibility. Choose the location around residency, latency and operating constraints, then select the platform.

Begin with the left-hand responsibility split. AWS manages supported Outposts infrastructure, while you provide site power, space and connectivity. Include both sides when planning availability and operational ownership.

Move to the second panel. Supported AWS workloads run near local systems and data. Check the services and capacity available for your chosen Outposts configuration rather than assuming the complete regional service catalog.

Follow the service-link arrows in the third panel. The Outpost connects to its parent Region for management and service communication. Include this dependency when designing connectivity and recovery.

Return to the complete slide and the disconnected example. Some existing local workloads can continue during a service-link interruption, while management operations and regional dependencies may be impaired. Test your application's actual dependency chain.

Follow the service link in the first panel. It connects an Outposts rack to the parent Region and carries the control-plane path. Treat regional connectivity as a separate requirement from local application access.

Move to the local gateway in the second panel. This connects rack subnets with the on-premises network. Trace the application's local traffic through the correct route rather than confusing it with the service link.

Inspect the routing checklist. Coordinate addressing, BGP and supported routing modes with the customer network. Verify reachability in both directions, including the routes used by the local application.

With the full slide restored, notice the server distinction on the right. Outposts servers use local network interfaces for on-premises connectivity. Do not apply the rack local-gateway model to the server form factor.
Begin in the upper-left panel. Enable a supported Local Zone, then create a subnet there to extend your VPC. Resources in that subnet are placed in the Local Zone.
Move to the upper-right panel. Supported compute and storage can sit closer to users or local systems. Evaluate the full request path, including any dependencies that still run in the parent Region.
Inspect the lower-left checklist. Available services and instance choices vary by location. Confirm support for the specific Local Zone before committing the architecture or estimating capacity.

Return to the full diagram and the lower-right panel. Include regional services, data paths, recovery and cross-zone transfers in the latency and cost model. Nearby compute alone does not guarantee a faster end-to-end application.
